lecture.title: Pragmatics: Meaning in Context
lecture.scope: Lecture 8. Original scenarios specify circumstances needed for a single best interpretation. Missing contexts are not invented as facts, and background assumptions are not treated as guaranteed truths.
lecture.exam_alignment: Concept-based practice. No past paper or official examination blueprint was supplied.
lecture.answer_model: Single best answer. answer_id refers to an option id, not its displayed position. Preserve option ids when shuffling.
lecture.display_guidance: In learning mode, display explanation followed by example after the learner answers. Source slides and clarification notes can appear in a reference panel.
lecture.terminology: Maxims are applied to explicitly stated dimensions of an exchange. Illocutionary force is distinguished from form, volume, and actual effects. Deictic reference uses a supplied participant, place, and time anchor.

references.title: 7.3 What does this sentence mean? Entailments vs. implicatures
references.supports: An implicature is suggested in context rather than guaranteed by the sentence alone.

references.title: Communication Across Cultures
references.supports: Conversational maxims are expectations for interpreting communication and implied meaning rather than guarantees of literal observance.

references.title: 8.15 Summary (and further questions to consider)
references.supports: Presupposed content is presented as background or common ground, distinct from independent confirmation of actual truth.

clarifications.note: Pragmatics is broader than implicature. The semantics/pragmatics contrast is analytical rather than a settled history or a rule excluding every contextual question from semantics.
Car-related inferences require specified circumstances. The rental interpretation of the son-and-dog exchange is an explicitly hypothetical practice scenario, not recovered original information.
Mean can express intention, indication, value, significance, or lexical interpretation. Explaining ghost does not require an actual ghost referent.

Quantity is neither maximal detail nor minimal words. Scenario facts distinguish it from manner. Quality concerns belief and support, not infallibility. Recognizable irony is not automatically covert deception.

Force is not loudness. Quoting or reporting a performative verb need not perform its act. Institutional examples specify appropriate conditions; a communicative act is distinguished from its behavioral effects.
Presuppositions are not automatically true facts. The France sentence is analysed without asserting real-world satisfaction. Another has an explicitly relevant prior-cup context.
Metaphor is not meaningless semantic failure. Relevant comparisons are specified. The surgeon example is fictional language analysis, not an allegation about a real person.
The pronoun/ typo is read as I. Deictic expressions retain conventional use conditions while reference needs context. Calendar exercises supply their own anchors.

questions.question: What does pragmatics primarily study in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Pragmatics investigates utterances as part of communication. Its questions include speaker meaning, inference, participant relationships, and the situation of use.
questions.example: A statement about a cold room can function as a request to close a window.

options.text: Only the physical duration of speech sounds
Only the alphabetical ordering of vocabulary
How language is interpreted and used in context
Only the internal structure of written words

questions.question: What does meaning-in-use emphasize?
questions.explanation: A linguistic form contributes meaning, but its use can communicate additional information or perform an action. The situation helps identify that contribution.
questions.example: There is a car coming can warn someone approaching a road.

options.text: The number of times a word appears in a dictionary
A guarantee that the same sentence always performs the same act
What an expression communicates when used in a particular situation
The idea that context removes every conventional word meaning

questions.question: Which comparison most clearly distinguishes a semantic focus from a pragmatic focus?
questions.explanation: The distinction concerns analytical emphasis, not two unrelated systems. Communication can require both linguistic content and contextual inference.
questions.example: Knowing cold differs from recognizing why someone mentioned the room’s temperature.

options.text: Conventional expression meaning versus interpretation of a speaker’s use in context
Loudness versus vocal-fold vibration
Word length versus sentence length
Past tense versus plural number

questions.question: A student says “It is cold here” beside an open window, intending a request to close it. What is the pragmatic interpretation?
questions.explanation: The literal content concerns temperature, while the stated context supports a request. The intended action is inferred rather than directly commanded.
questions.example: There is no space here may similarly request moving an object.

options.text: The sentence must be an explicit imperative in form.
The student wants someone to close the window.
The utterance is necessarily about a future journey.
Cold has lost every temperature-related meaning.

questions.question: What does speaker meaning refer to in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Speaker meaning concerns the communicative act and intended interpretation. It may extend beyond what the words explicitly state.
questions.example: A speaker can mention an approaching car to warn rather than merely report traffic.

options.text: The physical position of the speaker’s tongue
Only whether every factual claim is true
Only the dictionary entry for the speaker’s name
What a speaker intends to communicate through an utterance

questions.question: Which description best introduces a conversational implicature?
questions.explanation: An implicature is suggested through communication rather than simply stated as the literal message. The inference must be supported by the situation.
questions.example: I have an early class tomorrow can imply declining a late invitation in a suitable exchange.

options.text: A meaning guaranteed solely by the number of words
The exact sound sequence recorded by a microphone
A plural ending written inside a noun
An additional message inferred from an utterance and its context

questions.question: A friend asks “Will you join us late tonight?” You reply “I have an early class tomorrow,” intending to decline. What is implied in this supplied context?
questions.explanation: The reply gives a reason from which the refusal is inferred. The question states the intended use rather than treating the inference as unavoidable in all contexts.
questions.example: I must leave early tomorrow can similarly support declining a late event.

options.text: You are not planning to join them late tonight.
Tomorrow means you have already attended the class.
You have explicitly stated the address of the class.
Every early class prevents every evening activity.

questions.question: Why should pragmatics not be defined as only the study of implicatures?
questions.explanation: Implicature is one topic in the lecture, not its entire scope. Deixis and actions performed by utterances raise additional questions.
questions.example: Identifying who I refers to is contextual even when no indirect message is intended.

options.text: It also investigates contextual reference, speech acts, presuppositions, and other aspects of use.
Context is unrelated to speech acts.
Implicatures can occur only in written dictionaries.
All pragmatic interpretation must be metaphorical.

questions.question: Why is a context-derived implication not automatically a guaranteed consequence of the sentence alone?
questions.explanation: The same sentence can support different additional messages in different situations. An inference needs evidence rather than a fixed sentence-to-intention rule.
questions.example: An approaching-car report can warn a pedestrian or announce an expected guest.

options.text: A contextual inference is always a spelling error.
Every implication must be unrelated to the words spoken.
It can depend on background assumptions and be revised when context changes.
Listeners can infer only what is explicitly stated word for word.

questions.question: How should the slides’ semantics-versus-pragmatics contrast be understood most carefully?
questions.explanation: The diagrams simplify an analytical distinction. They are not a complete history or a rule excluding every contextual question from semantic theory.
questions.example: A deictic expression has a conventional use and a context-dependent reference.

options.text: It separates conventional meaning and contextual use without denying that they interact.
Pragmatics makes all word meanings entirely private and random.
Semantics cannot contribute anything to interpreting an utterance.
A teaching diagram alone proves the complete history of both fields.

questions.question: What is linguistic context in the lecture’s introductory account?
questions.explanation: Earlier or surrounding language can provide referents and expectations. This differs from relying only on the physical situation or world knowledge.
questions.example: Introducing Ali can help identify a later use of he.

options.text: Only the temperature of the room
Only the speaker’s physical height
The dictionary order of nearby headwords
The surrounding discourse that helps interpret an expression

questions.question: What does situational context include in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The situation includes who communicates, where and when, and what participants take others to know. Not every available fact is relevant.
questions.example: A road-crossing situation can support a warning interpretation.

options.text: Only the printed words before a sentence
Only the number of consonants in an utterance
Only the grammatical suffixes inside a noun
Participants, circumstances, and relevant knowledge or beliefs

questions.question: After “Sara met Ali,” a speaker continues “He looked tired.” Which information most directly helps interpret he?
questions.explanation: The preceding discourse introduces a likely referent. Resolution may still need wider context when several candidates are possible.
questions.example: Introducing a person by name can support a later pronoun reference.

options.text: The number of letters in tired
The alphabetical position of Ali
The preceding linguistic context
The loudness of met

questions.question: A parent says “There is a car coming” while a child is about to step into the road. What interpretation is best supported?
questions.explanation: The crossing situation makes a warning relevant. The interpretation depends on what participants are doing, not on a new dictionary meaning of car.
questions.example: The same words may serve a different purpose when a visitor arrives.

options.text: A warning to avoid stepping into the road
A request to repair a parked car
A guaranteed instruction to put food on a table
A declaration naming a ship

questions.question: A family has agreed to serve food when its guests’ car arrives. Someone reports the expected car approaching. What additional message can the shared plan support?
questions.explanation: The inference depends on the supplied agreement and expectation. Without that background, a food-related instruction would not be established.
questions.example: A shared plan can let a short announcement trigger an understood action.

options.text: Every approaching car always signals that food must be served.
Car now literally means dinner.
It may be time to prepare to serve the food.
A child must be standing in the road.

questions.question: Why does “There is a car coming” not always mean “put the food on the table”?
questions.explanation: The literal report can remain the same while its contextual function changes. The slide illustrates possibilities, not fixed equivalences.
questions.example: At a crossing, the purpose may be warning rather than announcing guests.

options.text: Food is an obligatory grammatical object of car.
That instruction depends on a particular shared situation or plan.
Every sentence has only one communicative purpose.
The instruction is directly expressed by coming.

questions.question: Suppose a landlord discussing a room does not allow pets. An applicant says “I also have a dog,” and the landlord replies “I’m sorry.” What makes a refusal interpretation plausible?
questions.explanation: The scenario explicitly supplies a context. It does not claim that the slide’s isolated dialogue proves this situation by itself.
questions.example: A shared restriction can explain an otherwise puzzling response.

options.text: The supplied rental situation and no-pets rule
The number of words in the reply
The presence of a first-person pronoun alone
A dictionary definition of sorry as dog

questions.question: Why should the isolated son-and-dog dialogue not be assigned one certain interpretation without more context?
questions.explanation: A plausible practice scenario must be identified as a hypothesis, not recovered as a fact from missing information.
questions.example: A rental setting can be supplied without claiming it was the original setting.

options.text: Every mention of a dog automatically refuses a rental application.
The dialogue contains no linguistic meanings.
Fourteen necessarily identifies the speaker’s profession.
Several situations could explain the responses, so a reading requires assumptions.

questions.question: A speaker says “The usual place?” because both friends regularly meet at one café. What supports the reference?
questions.explanation: The speaker expects identifying information to be recoverable from common experience. Full naming is unnecessary in this context.
questions.example: Our classroom may be identifiable to classmates without a room number.

options.text: The exact duration of the vowel in usual
An assumption of shared knowledge about their routine
A requirement that every listener know every café
The word place having no conventional meaning

questions.question: What does relative distance concern in the lecture’s introductory description of pragmatics?
questions.explanation: The expression can concern familiarity, respect, or formality. It need not be a physical distance measurement.
questions.example: A formal request may acknowledge a distant or respectful relationship.

options.text: Only the distance a sound wave travels
How speakers manage closeness or social distance in interaction
Only the number of meters between chairs
Only the position of a suffix within a word

questions.question: In “He meant to write,” what does meant express?
questions.explanation: Mean has different uses. Here it describes an intention to act rather than defining a word.
questions.example: She meant to call means she intended to call.

options.text: Intended
Had a plural ending
Denoted a particular object
Was physically loud

questions.question: In the traffic-signal illustration “A green light means go,” what does means express?
questions.explanation: The example concerns a conventional signal. It is a language illustration, not complete guidance for every traffic situation.
questions.example: A signal can indicate an expected response through a shared convention.

options.text: Has personal emotional importance only
Defines the dictionary meaning of life
Signals or indicates an instruction under a convention
Guarantees safe movement regardless of circumstances

questions.question: In “Health means everything to her,” what sense of means is prominent?
questions.explanation: The phrase expresses value. It does not define health as literally identical to every object in the world.
questions.example: Family means a lot to him has a similar use.

options.text: Has great importance
Has the spelling of everything
Identifies a grammatical subject
Creates a legal declaration

questions.question: In “What is the meaning of life?” which sense is most relevant?
questions.explanation: The question asks about significance rather than simply requesting a dictionary entry. Its exact purpose still depends on context.
questions.example: What is the point of this project? also asks about purpose.

options.text: The pronunciation of the letter l
The plural inflection of life
The physical location of the speaker
Purpose or significance

questions.question: After a friend receives an award, “What does it mean to you?” most naturally asks about what?
questions.explanation: The situation makes the question about the person’s response. Context must also supply what it refers to.
questions.example: The friend might explain that the award recognizes years of effort.

options.text: Its personal significance or interpretation
The number of phonemes in award
The identity of every award recipient in history
The grammatical tense of receive

questions.question: Which task is most directly requested by “What does the word ghost mean?”
questions.explanation: A word can be explained without proving that an actual referent exists. Real-world reference alone is too restrictive as an explanation of all lexical meaning.
questions.example: A dictionary can explain unicorn without locating a living unicorn.

options.text: Identify the speaker’s emotional state with certainty
Measure the loudness of the question
Explain the word’s conventional meaning
Locate an actual ghost before offering an explanation

questions.question: Which mapping matches the lecture’s summary?
questions.explanation: The summary distinguishes levels and analytical focus. These areas interact rather than replace one another.
questions.example: A word meaning, phrase interpretation, and indirect request invite different questions.

options.text: Lexical semantics concerns words and morphemes; phrasal semantics concerns larger combinations; pragmatics concerns use in context.
Phrasal semantics is dictionary alphabetization, while pragmatics is word counting.
Lexical semantics concerns whole conversations; phrasal semantics concerns spelling.
Pragmatics measures sound intensity, while semantics measures duration.

questions.question: What does the set of examples with mean and meaning demonstrate?
questions.explanation: A word’s construction and situation matter. A single gloss does not automatically fit every example.
questions.example: Meant to leave differs from means a great deal to me.

options.text: Meaning always requires a visible physical referent.
Every use must have exactly the same interpretation.
Context never helps distinguish a word’s uses.
Their uses can concern intention, indication, value, significance, or lexical interpretation.

questions.question: Which maxim concerns providing as much information as the exchange requires?
questions.explanation: Quantity concerns the appropriate amount of information. The shortest response is not always sufficient.
questions.example: A location question may require both a building name and room number.

options.text: Relevance
Manner
Quantity
Quality

questions.question: Which maxim concerns truthfulness and adequate support for claims?
questions.explanation: Quality asks speakers not to present what they believe false or unsupported. It does not guarantee that every supported belief will prove correct.
questions.example: A speaker should not invent an answer while pretending to know.

options.text: Quality
Manner
Relevance
Quantity

questions.question: Which maxim concerns keeping a contribution connected to the exchange?
questions.explanation: Relevance concerns the connection between a response and the discussion. An indirect response can be relevant when the connection is inferable.
questions.example: An early class can be relevant to declining a late invitation.

options.text: Quantity
Relevance
Quality
Manner

questions.question: Which maxim concerns clarity, orderliness, and avoiding obscurity?
questions.explanation: Manner concerns expression and presentation. Clear organization matters even when facts are true and relevant.
questions.example: Directions are easier to follow when their steps are given in order.

options.text: Relevance
Quality
Quantity
Manner

questions.question: A student asks for an exam’s room and time. The respondent truthfully gives only the room, intentionally omitting the known time. Which maxim is most directly at issue?
questions.explanation: The answer is relevant and can be clear and true, but required information is missing. The scenario isolates sufficiency.
questions.example: Room 12, at nine supplies both requested details.

options.text: Quality
Relevance
Manner
Quantity

questions.question: An exchange needs only a room number. The speaker gives it with a long set of unnecessary but related details. Which maxim is most directly at issue?
questions.explanation: The issue is excess information relative to the specified need. Length alone would not establish the problem.
questions.example: Room 12 may suffice when the building is already known.

options.text: Relevance
Quantity
Manner
Quality

questions.question: A speaker knowingly gives a false exam date while presenting it as verified. Which maxim is most directly breached?
questions.explanation: The speaker presents a claim believed false. A response can be brief and on topic while failing this expectation.
questions.example: Inventing a result and reporting it as checked raises the same issue.

options.text: Relevance
Manner
Quantity
Quality

questions.question: Asked where the library is, a respondent discusses yesterday’s football score with no relevant shared connection. Which maxim is most directly at issue?
questions.explanation: The response does not address the topic or an inferable purpose. The scenario excludes a special connection that could make it relevant.
questions.example: A useful answer could identify the library or admit not knowing.

options.text: Quality
Manner
Quantity
Relevance

questions.question: A speaker gives all required correct directions but uses undefined jargon and a confusing order. Which maxim is most directly at issue?
questions.explanation: The content is specified as sufficient, accurate, and relevant. The problem lies in obscure presentation.
questions.example: Numbered directions in a clear sequence can improve the answer.

options.text: Quality
Quantity
Manner
Relevance

questions.question: Which contrast separates quantity from manner?
questions.explanation: A response can provide enough facts unclearly or present insufficient information clearly. These are distinguishable problems.
questions.example: A clear room number is insufficient if the time was also requested.

options.text: Quantity concerns truth; manner concerns topic relevance.
Quantity concerns needed information; manner concerns clarity and organization.
Quantity and manner are identical whenever a reply is short.
Quantity concerns word meanings; manner concerns sound duration.

questions.question: Which contrast separates quality from relevance?
questions.explanation: Accuracy and topical connection are separate concerns. The scenario must identify which creates the problem.
questions.example: A false exam time is on topic; a true football score may be off topic.

options.text: A true reply is always relevant to every exchange.
A reply can be on topic but false, or true but unrelated.
A relevant reply is guaranteed true.
Both maxims depend only on sentence length.

questions.question: Why is “always say as little as possible” not an accurate statement of quantity?
questions.explanation: Too little can be as unhelpful as too much. Shared knowledge and the request affect the required detail.
questions.example: A new visitor may need more than a room number.

options.text: The required detail is identical in every situation.
Quantity requires avoiding every factual detail.
Only one-word answers can be cooperative.
A response must provide enough information for its current purpose.

questions.question: During an obvious downpour, someone says “What perfect weather!” intending recognizable irony. Why is this not automatically a covert attempt to deceive?
questions.explanation: An apparent departure from literal truth can be made obvious to communicate indirectly. The scenario distinguishes this from a hidden lie.
questions.example: Great timing! can express criticism when lateness is mutually obvious.

options.text: Every ironic remark is a literal weather forecast.
The obvious mismatch can invite an ironic interpretation.
Irony removes all relevance to the situation.
The words have no conventional meanings.

questions.question: A speaker answers on reasonable evidence with a belief that later proves wrong. What is the most careful assessment of quality?
questions.explanation: The expectation concerns the speaker’s basis and presentation, not infallibility. The circumstances need investigation.
questions.example: A timetable may change after the speaker checks it accurately.

options.text: The error alone does not establish deliberate deception or inadequate evidence.
Quality guarantees perfect knowledge of future events.
Every error proves that the speaker knowingly lied.
A short answer cannot raise any question about evidence.

questions.question: A reply is knowingly false and unrelated to the question, but clear and of the requested length. Which pair of maxims is most directly at issue?
questions.explanation: The false claim raises quality, and the lack of a topic connection raises relevance. The supplied clarity and adequate length distinguish the other dimensions.
questions.example: One reply can raise more than one conversational issue without making the maxims identical.

options.text: Quantity and relevance
Quality and relevance
Quantity and manner
Quality and manner

questions.question: How are conversational maxims best treated in this lecture?
questions.explanation: The framework supports reasoning about exchanges. Actual communication can involve indirectness, obvious departures, or competing demands.
questions.example: A listener can recover an unstated message through shared context.

options.text: A list of grammatical suffixes
Rules proving every figurative expression meaningless
Interpretive expectations that help explain communication rather than guarantees of literal observance
Statutes imposing legal penalties for long replies

questions.question: What is the central idea of speech-act theory in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Promising, warning, betting, congratulating, and resigning can be acts in communication rather than merely descriptions.
questions.example: I promise to return the book can undertake a commitment.

options.text: Every utterance describes physical movement.
Only written sentences have communicative purposes.
Words cannot affect commitments or relationships.
People can perform actions through language.

questions.question: Said sincerely in an appropriate conversation, “I promise to return your book tomorrow” most directly performs which act?
questions.explanation: The speaker undertakes a future commitment. The scenario specifies a genuine use rather than a theatrical quotation.
questions.example: I promise to call can similarly make a promise.

options.text: Describing the book’s physical appearance
Asking how promise is spelled
Reporting a promise made last year
Promising

questions.question: A person indicates a dangerous step and says “I warn you: it is loose.” Which act is foregrounded?
questions.explanation: The utterance alerts a listener to a risk. Its purpose extends beyond a neutral report.
questions.example: Watch out, the floor is slippery can warn without using warn.

options.text: Resigning from office
Naming a ship
Warning
Defining loose in a dictionary

questions.question: What is illocutionary force in the lecture’s terminology?
questions.explanation: Force identifies an act such as warning or requesting, not a physical sound measurement.
questions.example: A quiet request can still have the force of a request.

options.text: The strength of vocal-fold vibration
The number of clauses in a sentence
The communicative act performed by an utterance
The utterance’s acoustic loudness

questions.question: Someone says “I resign” in a genuine, appropriate workplace procedure. Why is this performative?
questions.explanation: The act is undertaken through language in the specified setting. Quotation or rehearsal need not have that effect.
questions.example: An actor saying I resign in a play is a different use.

options.text: The sentence only defines a spelling.
The utterance is used to carry out the resignation act.
The speaker must be reporting another person’s past decision.
Resign is a question marker.

questions.question: In an agreed wager, a friend says “I bet you that our team will win.” Which speech act is foregrounded?
questions.explanation: The supplied context makes the utterance part of undertaking a bet, rather than merely reporting a belief about the team. Different verbs can identify different acts.
questions.example: I nominate Sara for the position would perform a nomination in an appropriate procedure.

options.text: Betting
Swearing testimony
Nominating a candidate
Offering congratulations

questions.question: Why does performing a warning not require the listener actually to obey?
questions.explanation: A warning can be issued even when ignored. Whether it changes behavior requires separate evidence.
questions.example: A person can warn about rain even if the listener takes no umbrella.

options.text: A warning exists only if it changes behavior.
The communicative act and its intended effect are distinct questions.
An ignored warning becomes an adjective phrase.
A warning must always be shouted.

questions.question: An authorized celebrant uses the required declaration in a valid marriage ceremony. What makes this relevant to speech acts?
questions.explanation: Authority and setting help determine the act’s status. The same wording in rehearsal need not produce the institutional result.
questions.example: An appropriate judicial declaration similarly depends on its setting.

options.text: Any mention of marriage automatically creates one.
The words participate in an institutional act under appropriate conditions.
The declaration is only a dictionary definition.
Institutional circumstances cannot affect an utterance.

questions.question: Why is a performative verb’s presence insufficient to prove that its act is performed now?
questions.explanation: Mentioning an act and doing it are different. Grammatical construction and communicative use matter.
questions.example: She promised yesterday describes a past act without itself making that promise.

options.text: All acts require an identical formula.
Every occurrence of promise commits the current speaker.
It may occur in a report, quotation, denial, or hypothetical example.
Warn cannot describe an earlier event.

questions.question: A friend quietly asks “Could you stay until I feel better?” intending a request. Which analysis keeps form, force, and volume separate?
questions.explanation: Structure, communicative act, and physical delivery are different dimensions. The supplied situation supports a request in question form.
questions.example: Can you help me? can also be a softly spoken request.

options.text: Imperative form solely because a request is intended
Interrogative form, request force, and quiet delivery
A force consisting of acoustic intensity alone
No speech act because the voice is quiet

questions.question: What is a presupposition in the introductory account used here?
questions.explanation: Presupposed content is backgrounded rather than introduced as the main point. Being assumed does not guarantee truth.
questions.example: Sara stopped writing poems normally backgrounds earlier writing.

options.text: Background information an utterance presents as already assumed
Only the action explicitly commanded
The physical duration of an utterance
Any claim independently proven true

questions.question: In “Have you stopped hugging your sheepdog?” what earlier activity is normally presupposed by stopped?
questions.explanation: The question backgrounds an earlier activity while asking whether it ceased. It does not independently verify that background.
questions.example: Have you stopped smoking? similarly assumes earlier smoking in its ordinary use.

options.text: The question proves you stopped yesterday.
You have never hugged an animal.
The dog promised to hug you.
You previously hugged the sheepdog.

questions.question: What is normally presupposed by “John does not write poems anymore”?
questions.explanation: Anymore relates a present negative claim to an earlier activity or state. The earlier activity is distinguished from the current assertion.
questions.example: She does not work there anymore normally suggests earlier employment.

options.text: John used to write poems.
John now writes poems every day.
John has never written anything.
John must be writing a novel now.

questions.question: A guest has finished a cup of tea. The host asks “Would you like another cup?” What background is continued by another here?
questions.explanation: Another presents the offered cup as additional to a relevant earlier one. The explicit scenario fixes the interpretation.
questions.example: Another slice can similarly refer to an additional portion.

options.text: A previous cup has been part of the relevant situation.
The guest is obliged to accept.
The guest has never encountered tea.
The host has guaranteed the guest wants more.

questions.question: Consider “The present king of France is bald” as a classic example without assuming it true. Which existential assumption is traditionally discussed?
questions.explanation: The question analyses an assumed referent without asserting that the actual world satisfies it. A listener can challenge such background.
questions.example: A definite description can invite an existence assumption.

options.text: The speaker is the king.
There is a contextually identifiable present king of France.
Every king is bald.
Bald must mean a type of crown.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to define presuppositions simply as facts?
questions.explanation: Presupposition concerns how content is presented. Its truth and acceptance are separate issues.
questions.example: A listener can reject the assumption that they own a dog.

options.text: A speaker can presuppose something false, disputed, or unshared.
Every background assumption is guaranteed correct.
A false assumption prevents analysis of the wording.
Presuppositions cannot occur in questions.

questions.question: Asked “Have you stopped hugging your sheepdog?”, someone replies “I have never had a sheepdog.” What is the response doing?
questions.explanation: The reply rejects assumed background and avoids accepting it through an inappropriate yes-or-no answer.
questions.example: I never smoked can challenge Have you stopped smoking?

options.text: Defining the word hug
Accepting every assumption of the question
Challenging a background assumption rather than merely answering yes or no
Promising to acquire a dog

questions.question: Which analysis separates background from the main assertion in “Sara stopped writing poems”?
questions.explanation: The ordinary analysis distinguishes what is taken for granted from the update. Special contexts can still require attention.
questions.example: No longer works there similarly updates a state against earlier employment.

options.text: The sentence necessarily says Sara will restart tomorrow.
Both are claims about sound intensity.
Earlier writing is backgrounded; cessation is the main asserted change.
Cessation is backgrounded; earlier writing is the only current assertion.

questions.question: How can a loaded question mislead even without supplying its answer?
questions.explanation: The question format can conceal a commitment in the background. A respondent may need to challenge it before answering.
questions.example: When did you stop cheating? backgrounds alleged earlier cheating without proving it.

options.text: Only declaratives contain meaningful words.
Questions cannot communicate background information.
Every question literally asserts that its answer is yes.
It can invite acceptance of a disputed background assumption.

questions.question: Which distinction separates declining through “I have an early class” from the stopped-writing example?
questions.explanation: The examples foreground different kinds of meaning. Implication and presupposed background should not be collapsed into one label.
questions.example: A speaker can imply refusal without using a cessation expression.

options.text: Both are direct commands.
Both are guaranteed true because they are spoken.
The first has no conventional meaning and the second has no context.
The refusal is a contextual inference; earlier writing is backgrounded by cessation.

questions.question: What is the central contrast in the lecture’s metaphor discussion?
questions.explanation: An expression can be used beyond its literal category application to convey a selected resemblance. This need not be random nonsense.
questions.example: Calling a determined person a tiger can highlight a relevant quality.

options.text: A plural form versus a singular form
Literal category application versus a figurative interpretation through comparison
A high-frequency sound versus a low-frequency sound
A preposition versus its printed font

questions.question: A speaker calls Jack “a tiger” specifically to praise courage in a difficult contest. Which interpretation fits?
questions.explanation: The supplied context identifies the comparison. It does not require literal species membership.
questions.example: Calling someone a lion can similarly highlight courage in a stated context.

options.text: Jack literally became a different species.
Jack names every tiger in the world.
Tiger has lost every conventional association.
Jack acted courageously or fiercely.

questions.question: Someone says “Walls have ears” to warn a companion about being overheard. What is intended?
questions.explanation: The conventional figurative expression supports a warning in the situation. It does not require a literal anatomical claim.
questions.example: Be careful what you say makes the warning explicit.

options.text: Every mention of walls is a biological report.
The wall has been appointed an official witness.
Others may be listening, so the speakers should be cautious.
Literal ears have been verified growing on the building.

questions.question: In a fictional example, a critic calls a surgeon “a butcher” to condemn rough work. What makes this use metaphorical?
questions.explanation: The context specifies a critical comparison. This is language analysis, not a factual allegation about a real clinician.
questions.example: Calling someone a machine can highlight a quality without literal identity.

options.text: An occupation term figuratively characterizes the surgeon’s work.
The critic necessarily identifies a second literal occupation.
Butcher has become a plural suffix.
The statement can only offer meat for sale.

questions.question: Why must a metaphor question supply enough context?
questions.explanation: A metaphor does not transfer every property of its source. The situation guides which qualities are relevant.
questions.example: Tiger can highlight courage in one context and aggression in another.

options.text: Word count alone determines figurative meaning.
Context deletes all literal meanings from the language.
The relevant comparison can differ across uses of the expression.
Every metaphor has one interpretation in every situation.

questions.question: Why is metaphor not adequately described as meaningless breaking of semantic rules?
questions.explanation: The lecture’s stretching description should not imply meaningless failure. Shared associations and context can support interpretation.
questions.example: Our doubts are traitors presents doubt as working against us.

options.text: Figurative interpretation can be systematic and intelligible.
Every literal mismatch has no possible interpretation.
Metaphor always creates a tense ending.
A comparison is understandable only if literally true.

questions.question: What is deixis?
questions.explanation: Deictic interpretation needs an anchor such as speaker, place, or time. The expressions retain conventional uses.
questions.example: I, here, and tomorrow require contextual anchoring.

options.text: The measurement of speech intensity
Context-dependent reference anchored to an utterance situation
A rule requiring a plural suffix on every noun
A dictionary alphabetization method

questions.question: Which group consists of person-deictic expressions in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Person deixis concerns participant-related reference. Identifying the speaker and addressee helps recover it.
questions.example: My ordinarily relates a possession or association to the speaker.

options.text: now, tomorrow, and yesterday
table, river, and window
I, you, and my
here, there, and nearby

questions.question: Sara says to Ali, “I will help you.” Who do I and you refer to?
questions.explanation: The supplied participants anchor the pronouns. The same wording can identify different people when speaker roles change.
questions.example: If Ali replies I will help you, their mapping changes.

options.text: Both refer to any person listed in a dictionary.
The pronouns have no possible reference in a future sentence.
I is Sara, and you is Ali.
I is Ali, and you is Sara.

questions.question: Which expression most clearly illustrates place deixis?
questions.explanation: Over there directs attention to a location in the situation. Person and time expressions require different anchors.
questions.example: This place can require a shared location or gesture.

options.text: now
over there
mine
tomorrow

questions.question: A teacher points to one of several towers and says “That tower is old.” What helps identify the tower?
questions.explanation: The noun supplies a category, while the demonstrative use needs identification. A gesture can help establish the referent.
questions.example: That book can be identified by pointing to a particular book.

options.text: The age of every teacher in the school
The shared situation and pointing gesture
The alphabetical position of tower
The past tense of an absent verb

questions.question: Which set most clearly illustrates time deixis?
questions.explanation: These expressions locate time relative to the utterance or another supplied reference point. Exact dates need an appropriate anchor.
questions.example: Tomorrow ordinarily identifies the day after the utterance day.

options.text: teacher, student, and classroom
now, tomorrow, and two weeks from now
those towers, this city, and over there
mine, yours, and ours

questions.question: Under an ordinary utterance-day interpretation, someone says on 10 March “I will return tomorrow.” Which date is indicated?
questions.explanation: The stated day anchors tomorrow. The answer does not depend on the reader’s current date.
questions.example: Spoken on 12 March, the same sentence ordinarily points to 13 March.

options.text: 24 March
10 March
9 March
11 March

questions.question: Why does I not lack semantic meaning just because it refers to different speakers?
questions.explanation: A stable use rule can yield different referents across utterances. Context identifies the participant satisfying that rule.
questions.example: Sara’s I and Ali’s I follow the same rule but identify different people.

options.text: Context-dependent expressions cannot be interpreted.
Each occurrence has a wholly unrelated dictionary definition.
Only names have conventional meanings.
Its conventional use identifies the speaker, while context determines who that is.

questions.question: Why is an account of deixis incomplete if it says context matters but ignores conventional meaning?
questions.explanation: Context works with linguistic information rather than replacing it. Person, place, and time expressions guide different interpretations.
questions.example: Tomorrow guides a time interpretation rather than naming a physical object.

options.text: Linguistic conventions constrain the kind of reference context supplies.
Here must refer to a person whenever one is mentioned.
Deictic expressions have no conventional use patterns.
Tomorrow can mean any object without a special reinterpretation.

questions.question: Sara tells Ali on Monday in their classroom, “I will meet you here tomorrow.” Which mapping follows the supplied context?
questions.explanation: Speaker, addressee, location, and day anchor the expressions together. The classroom is supplied for this example, not a universal referent of here.
questions.example: Repeating the sentence elsewhere on another day can change its references.

options.text: I is Ali, you is Sara, here must be a station, and tomorrow is Sunday.
I is an absent teacher, and tomorrow is Monday.
I is Sara, you is Ali, here is the relevant classroom location, and tomorrow is Tuesday.
Here names every classroom, and you always refers to Sara.
